source_reviews.independent_solution: A tetrahedron has the minimum four faces, six edges, four vertices and zero polyhedron diagonals. In a convex polyhedron each face has at least three edges, and each adjacent face can share at most one edge with it, so at least three other faces are needed. source_reviews.independent_solution: A five-faced convex polyhedron can have a quadrilateral face: a square-based pyramid has a square and four triangular faces. It cannot have a pentagonal face: the five edges of that face must border five distinct other faces (two convex faces cannot share two distinct edges), requiring at least six faces. The question is whether a face can have each polygon type, not whether all five faces are quadrilaterals.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Minimum 12 edges. The hexagonal face already contributes six edges. Each of its six vertices must have an incident edge not lying in that face because a solid polyhedron vertex has degree at least three. An additional edge cannot join two of those vertices: it would lie in the face plane, either duplicate a boundary edge or run through the interior of the face. Thus six distinct outgoing edges are necessary, in addition to the six boundary edges. A hexagonal pyramid realizes exactly six base edges and six lateral edges.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The intersection statement is true: if X,Y lie in both convex solids, the entire segment XY lies in each and hence in their intersection; the hypothesis excludes an intersection that is not a solid polyhedron. The union statement is false. Let P=[0,2]x[0,1]x[0,1] and Q=[0,1]x[0,2]x[0,1]. These are convex boxes; their union is an L-shaped prism and is a polyhedron. X=(2,1,1/2) lies in P and Y=(1,2,1/2) lies in Q, while their midpoint (3/2,3/2,1/2) lies in neither. Thus the union is not convex.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Take a>0, A=(0,0,0), B=(a,0,0), C=(a,a,0), D=(0,a,0). ABEF is an isosceles trapezoid in the plane perpendicular to ABC along AB, with AB parallel EF, AB=a and EF=AF=BE=a/2. Each horizontal end offset is (a-a/2)/2=a/4, so its height is h=sqrt((a/2)^2-(a/4)^2)=sqrt(3)a/4. Choose F=(a/4,0,h), E=(3a/4,0,h); reflection across ABC leaves all requested values unchanged. For AF, sin(alpha)=h/(a/2)=sqrt(3)/2, giving alpha=60 degrees. CDF meets ABC along CD; a cross-section perpendicular to CD has horizontal distance a and vertical rise h, so tan(beta)=h/a=sqrt(3)/4 and beta=arctan(sqrt(3)/4), the acute plane angle. The five faces are ABCD, ABEF, DCEF, ADF and BCE. Their areas are a^2, 3sqrt(3)a^2/16, 3sqrt(19)a^2/16, a^2/4, a^2/4 respectively: DCEF has bases a and a/2 and in-plane height sqrt(a^2+h^2)=sqrt(19)a/4; each side triangle has base a and perpendicular height sqrt((a/4)^2+h^2)=a/2. Total net area equals total surface area, 3a^2(8+sqrt(3)+sqrt(19))/16; cutting/unfolding changes no area. No length unit is supplied, so the result is in squared units corresponding to a.
